newsitem.title: CHINA: Paroled Tibetan monk said under house arrest.
newsitem.headline: Paroled Tibetan monk said under house arrest.

text.p: A 68-year-old Tibetan monk and leading dissident, on parole after nearly three decades in prison, is under effective house arrest, the London-based Tibet Information Network said.

Yulo Dawa Tsering was under guard or regularly visited by police in Tibet's capital, Lhasa, the group said in a statement seen by Reuters on Monday, quoting members of the European Parliament who met him last week.

The monk was under virtual house arrest apparently as punishment for speaking to a visiting U.N. human rights delegation two years ago, said the group, which monitors the human rights situation in the Himalayan region.

"They (Chinese officials) said he was on parole but during the meeting it appeared to us that this was not parole in our sense of the word," the group quoted Bernie Malone, an Irish member of the European Parliament, as saying.
"He appeared to be under some kind of restraint -- he did not have the freedom to come or go," said Malone, who could speak to the monk for a maximum of 10 minutes.
"He was not the master of his own movements," she said.

Yulo Dawa Tsering had been sentenced to life imprisonment in 1959, but was released under an amnesty 20 years later, according to "Detained in China and Tibet", a directory of political and religious prisoners.
It gave no details of the charges against the monk.
He was jailed for 10 years in 1989 for spreading counter-revolutionary, or subversive, propaganda, "Detained in China and Tibet" said.

The monk vilified policies of the Communist Party and spread "reactionary" views on subjects such as Tibetan independence to foreign visitors, "Detained in China and Tibet" said. The monk was paroled from that jail term two years ago.
Tibet Information Network said the European MPs visited Lhasa last week and met Yulo Dawa Tsering amid tight security and on condition that they took no photographs of him.
Officials reached by telephone in Lhasa declined to comment on the report.

It was the first time the monk had been seen by foreigners since November 1994 when he gave an on-the-record statement to M. Abdelfattah Amor, the United Nations' investigator into religious intolerance, during an official U.N. mission to China and Tibet, it said.
Many Tibetan monks and nuns are loyal to their spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, who fled into exile in India in 1959 after an abortive uprising against the Chinese.
The Dalai Lama won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his non-violent campaign for autonomy for his homeland, but Beijing suspects he is seeking to split Tibet from China.
